title: Database Migrations with Flyway
intro: A production database schema should not be modified manually or at application startup. In this lesson, you will learn how to safely manage schema changes with versioned Flyway migrations in development, testing, and production.
body:
## Why do we need database migrations?

Your application's database schema will change over time.

Today, for example, the `tasks` table may only have `id`, `title`, and `done` fields. Later, you may want to add a priority:

~~~text
V1
  tasks(id, title, done)

V2
  tasks(id, title, done, priority)
~~~

On a development machine, it may seem simple to run an SQL statement:

~~~sql
ALTER TABLE tasks ADD COLUMN priority TEXT;
~~~

In production, however, more serious questions arise.

What exactly happened to the database? Which developer ran the change? Did the same thing happen in the test environment? When setting up a new instance, which SQL statements need to be run? How does a new team member know what state the database should be in?

Migrations provide a structured solution to these problems.

A migration is a **versioned, reproducible database change**. Instead of the process of getting the database from one state to another living in documentation or in a developer's head, the change itself becomes part of the source code.

~~~text
V1 -> V2 -> V3 -> V4 -> ...
~~~

This means a new environment can run the same migrations in the same order.

### Why is this especially important in a team?

Imagine that five of you are working on the same backend project. If everyone manually modifies their local database, after a few weeks you can easily end up with different schemas.

Migrations instead say:

> The current structure of the database is the result of the versioned migrations.

This can be stored in the Git repository just like the Java code.

Migrations are especially important:

- when multiple developers are working on the project,
- in CI/CD environments,
- in staging and production environments,
- when creating a new server or database,
- when planning rollback and release processes.

And the production database is not the place where we experiment with SQL manually.

---

## Flyway in a Spring Boot application

In the Java/Spring Boot world, one commonly used migration tool is **Flyway**.

With Maven, you will need the Flyway core package:

~~~xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.flywaydb</groupId>
    <artifactId>flyway-core</artifactId>
</dependency>
~~~

When using PostgreSQL, also add PostgreSQL support:

~~~xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.flywaydb</groupId>
    <artifactId>flyway-database-postgresql</artifactId>
</dependency>
~~~

With Spring Boot, the exact versions are generally managed by Spring Boot's dependency management, so you do not need to specify a separate version for every dependency.

---

## Where are the migration files?

Flyway's default migration directory in Spring Boot is:

~~~text
src/main/resources/db/migration
~~~

For example:

~~~text
src/
└── main/
    └── resources/
        └── db/
            └── migration/
                ├── V1__create_tasks.sql
                └── V2__add_priority.sql
~~~

The filenames have meaning.

~~~text
V1__create_tasks.sql
^^
version
~~~

`V1` is the migration version.

After the two underscores (`__`) comes a human-readable description:

~~~text
V1__create_tasks.sql
   ^^^^^^^^^^^^
   description
~~~

The next migration could be:

~~~text
V2__add_priority.sql
~~~

Then:

~~~text
V3__create_task_comments.sql
~~~

It is worth keeping filenames short but clear.

---

## How does Flyway know what has already run?

Flyway does not blindly run all SQL files again every time the application starts.

~~~diagram
{"type": "flow", "title": "How Flyway decides what to run", "nodes": [{"id": "files", "label": "db/migration/", "sub": "V1__init · V2__tags · V3__index", "kind": "file"}, {"id": "fw", "label": "Flyway at startup", "kind": "service", "highlight": true}, {"id": "hist", "label": "flyway_schema_history", "sub": "V1 ✓ · V2 ✓ (checksums)", "kind": "db"}, {"id": "run", "label": "Run V3 only", "sub": "then record it", "highlight": true}], "edges": [{"from": "files", "to": "fw"}, {"from": "hist", "to": "fw", "label": "already applied"}, {"from": "fw", "to": "run"}]}
~~~

It creates its own table, which by default is:

~~~text
flyway_schema_history
~~~

Among other things, this stores the version, description, and status of executed migrations.

A simplified view:

~~~text
flyway_schema_history

version | description       | success
--------|-------------------|--------
1       | create_tasks      | true
2       | add_priority      | true
3       | create_comments   | true
~~~

When the application starts, Flyway compares the migrations in the project with the state recorded in the database.

For example, if the database has only reached V1, but V2 and V3 already exist in the project, Flyway can apply these missing migrations in the correct order.

This makes it possible for the same repository to gradually bring different environments to the same schema.

### Checksums

Flyway also uses checksums for migration files.

This is an important safety mechanism. If you later change the SQL of a migration that has already been executed, the file's contents no longer match what Flyway previously executed.

Flyway can detect this and report a migration validation error.

This leads to one of Flyway's most important rules.

---

## The golden rule: do not modify an executed migration

**If a migration has already run on a shared or production database, do not edit the file.**

Suppose this already exists:

~~~text
V1__create_tasks.sql
~~~

and it has already run in production.

Later, you realize that you need a new field.

Do not do this:

~~~text
V1__create_tasks.sql  <- modified
~~~

Instead, create a new one:

~~~text
V2__add_priority.sql
~~~

For example:

~~~sql
ALTER TABLE tasks
ADD COLUMN priority TEXT;
~~~

The Git history then also preserves how the schema evolved.

~~~text
V1: created the tasks table
       |
       v
V2: added the priority field
       |
       v
V3: created the task_tags relationship
~~~

This migration history is part of the application's history.

### Why is modifying an old migration a problem?

Suppose V1 has already run on your machine, but a new developer clones the repository tomorrow.

If you modify V1, the new developer would run different SQL as V1 from what your database originally received.

In production, the situation is even worse: the old migration has already happened there, so changing the source file does not automatically change the existing database.

**New database change = new migration.**

---

## Safely changing the schema with existing data

Changing a database becomes particularly interesting when it already contains data.

Suppose you have a `tasks` table with several million records, and you want to add a required `priority` field.

As a first attempt, it may be tempting to do this:

~~~sql
ALTER TABLE tasks
ADD COLUMN priority TEXT NOT NULL;
~~~

This can be problematic because the existing rows do not have a value for this new required field.

A safer strategy may be to make the change over several releases.

### Step 1: add a nullable field

First, add it in a way that remains valid alongside the existing data:

~~~sql
ALTER TABLE tasks
ADD COLUMN priority TEXT;
~~~

### Step 2: backfill

**Backfill** means populating the existing records with a value for the new field.

~~~sql
UPDATE tasks
SET priority = 'normal'
WHERE priority IS NULL;
~~~

### Step 3: NOT NULL

Once every existing record has received an appropriate value, you can make the field required in the next migration.

The exact SQL may depend on the PostgreSQL version and the constraint strategy you want to use, so this needs to be planned especially carefully for large tables.

Another option is to provide a default value in the first migration:

~~~sql
ALTER TABLE tasks
ADD COLUMN priority TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'normal';
~~~

In this case, the new column has a meaningful default value.

The appropriate strategy depends on the size of the table, the database version you use, how much downtime is acceptable, and how you deploy the application.

---

## Safely renaming columns

Renaming a column seems simple at first:

~~~diagram
{"type": "steps", "title": "Rename a column without downtime", "steps": [{"label": "V5: add", "sub": "new column, nullable"}, {"label": "Deploy app", "sub": "writes both columns"}, {"label": "V6: backfill", "sub": "copy old → new"}, {"label": "Deploy app", "sub": "reads new only"}, {"label": "V7: drop", "sub": "remove old column"}]}
~~~

~~~sql
ALTER TABLE tasks
RENAME COLUMN title TO task_title;
~~~

But in a running production system, the application and database are not necessarily updated at the same time.

If the old backend is still trying to access the column as `title`, while the new schema only contains it as `task_title`, the application will fail.

For this reason, larger systems often use the so-called **expand-and-contract** strategy.

First, you add the new structure while the old one still works. Then you switch the application to the new structure. Finally, in a later migration, you can remove the old structure.

~~~text
Release 1: old + new structure
          |
          v
Release 2: application now uses the new structure
          |
          v
Release 3: old structure removed
~~~

This is especially important in a rolling deployment or a production system consisting of multiple instances.

---

## Dropping columns and tables

`DROP COLUMN` or `DROP TABLE` can be much more dangerous than adding a new column.

For example:

~~~sql
ALTER TABLE tasks
DROP COLUMN old_field;
~~~

If the running application still uses this column, you can get an immediate error.

Therefore, before deleting something, you generally first remove its use from the code, deploy the new version, verify that the old data is no longer needed, and only then delete it from the database.

With production migrations, think in terms of releases, not just SQL statements.

---

## Repeatable migrations

Flyway also supports **repeatable migrations**, whose filenames start with the `R__` prefix, for example `R__create_reporting_view.sql`. These are not classic, one-time versions: Flyway tracks the checksum of their contents and can apply them again when the file changes. They can be useful, for example, for managing views or other database objects that can always be regenerated from their current definition.

---

## Flyway and Hibernate together

You now have two separate mechanisms for managing the database schema.

One is Flyway:

~~~text
Java project
   |
   +-- V1 migration
   +-- V2 migration
   +-- V3 migration
   |
   v
PostgreSQL schema
~~~

The other is Hibernate's automatic schema management.

In production, you do not want both of them independently trying to modify the database.

Therefore, it is worth putting Hibernate into validation mode:

~~~properties
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate
~~~

`validate` does not try to modify the schema. Instead, it checks whether the structure expected by Hibernate is consistent with the database.

This makes the responsibilities clear:

~~~text
Flyway
  -> creates and modifies the schema

Hibernate/JPA
  -> uses and validates the schema
~~~

During development, you may encounter the `ddl-auto=update` setting because it is convenient. In production, however, controlled migrations are the better approach.

A typical production configuration is therefore, for example:

~~~properties
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate
spring.jpa.show-sql=false
~~~

The actual logging configuration should of course be handled separately for each environment.

---

## A complete migration process

Let's look at what a simple evolution process might look like.

### V1

You create the initial `tasks` table:

~~~sql
CREATE TABLE tasks (
    id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    title TEXT NOT NULL,
    done BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE
);
~~~

### V2

You add a new field:

~~~sql
ALTER TABLE tasks
ADD COLUMN priority TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'normal';
~~~

### V3

You introduce a new relationship:

~~~sql
CREATE TABLE tags (
    id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
);
~~~

Then you create the join table representing the relationship.

Each step is a separate migration that is added to the Git repository.

If a new developer creates an empty PostgreSQL database, Flyway can apply the migrations one by one:

~~~text
V1 -> V2 -> V3
~~~

If a production database is already at V2, only the missing V3 needs to be applied.

This is one of the most important advantages of migration-based database management.

---

## Common mistakes

### Modifying an executed migration

This is one of the most important rules to remember. If a migration has already run on a shared or production database, do not edit it. Create a new version.

### Manual SQL in production

A quick manual fix may seem like an easy solution, but later it will not be part of the repository's migration history. As a result, the change may be missing from other environments.

### Breaking the application and database at the same time

Immediately renaming or deleting a column can cause problems if the old application version still uses it. Use a multi-step, backward-compatible transition when necessary.

### `ddl-auto=update` in production

Hibernate schema update is convenient during development, but it does not replace versioned migrations in production.

### Skipping migration testing

A migration is also code. Run it through in a test or staging environment with real, preferably representative data before it reaches production.

---

## Summary

With Flyway, the database schema becomes a versioned artifact just like the Java code itself.

The most important rules are:

- every schema change should be a migration,
- migrations should be versioned and stored in Git,
- do not edit an executed migration,
- when existing data is involved, plan the change in multiple steps,
- do not modify the production database manually with SQL,
- let Flyway manage schema changes,
- with Hibernate, use the `ddl-auto=validate` approach in production.

In the next lesson, we will no longer look at how to change the schema, but at how database queries perform. We will look at indexes, using `EXPLAIN`, and how to find the real cause of slow SQL queries.
takeaways: Flyway manages database schema changes with versioned and reproducible migrations.
An executed migration must not be modified; every new schema change should appear in a new migration.
When modifying existing data, it is often safer to make the change gradually over several releases.
Do not modify the production database manually; manage it through migrations versioned in Git.
Alongside Flyway, Hibernate can use `ddl-auto=validate` to check whether the entity model matches the managed database schema.

quiz.question: What is the most important reason for managing a production database schema with versioned migrations?
options: This allows Hibernate to create entities faster
This makes schema changes reproducible and allows them to be applied consistently across different environments
This means you no longer need SQL knowledge
This makes PostgreSQL automatically restore every deletion
quiz.explanation: Migrations are versioned, reproducible changes stored in source code, so development, test, and production environments can be brought to the same schema state.

quiz.question: What happens if you later modify the SQL content of an already executed V2 migration?
options: Flyway automatically turns it into a new V3 migration
PostgreSQL automatically rolls back the previous V2
Its checksum may differ, and Flyway may report a validation error
Nothing, because Flyway does not check the contents of migration files
quiz.explanation: Flyway can use checksums to detect whether the contents of a migration file that has already been applied have changed.

quiz.question: Which filename represents a traditional versioned Flyway migration?
options: migration_add_priority.sql
R__add_priority.sql
V2__add_priority.sql
M2__add_priority.sql
quiz.explanation: A versioned Flyway migration uses a format such as `V2__add_priority.sql`. The `R__` prefix indicates a repeatable migration.

quiz.question: Why can it be dangerous to directly add a NOT NULL column to an already populated table?
options: Because NOT NULL always deletes existing rows
Because the existing rows do not necessarily have a value for the new required column
Because PostgreSQL does not support NOT NULL columns
Because Flyway cannot run ALTER TABLE statements
quiz.explanation: Existing records also need a valid value for the new required field. That is why adding a nullable field, backfilling it, and then tightening the constraint is often the safer strategy.

quiz.question: What does using `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate` alongside Flyway mean?
options: Hibernate modifies the schema on every startup based on the entities
Hibernate deletes the database and creates it again
Hibernate checks whether the entity model matches the database schema, but does not modify it
Flyway runs every migration twice
quiz.explanation: `validate` checks that the schema and entity model are consistent, while the actual schema changes are left to Flyway migrations.

exercise.title: V2 migration: priorities and tags
exercise.task: The starting database is after the V1 migration. Write the V2 migration SQL. Add a `priority` column to the tasks table that is of type TEXT, required, has a default value of `normal`, and only allows `low`, `normal`, or `high` values. Create the `tags` table with an `id` and a unique, required `name` field. Then create the `task_tags` join table, where a task-tag relationship can only appear once, and both foreign keys use CASCADE deletion. Finally, insert the `work` and `home` tags. The exercise runs in a SQLite environment, so identity and some ALTER TABLE capabilities differ from PostgreSQL. In production, you use PostgreSQL, where the schema and ALTER TABLE capabilities are broader. The migration must work so that the four tasks already present in V1 are preserved, and each receives the `normal` priority.
exercise.hint: The existing tasks must survive the column addition, so provide a default `normal` value. Restrict the allowed priority values with a CHECK constraint. In the task_tags table, the composite PRIMARY KEY `(task_id, tag_id)` alongside the two foreign keys ensures that the same relationship cannot appear twice.

tests.name: Existing tasks remain with normal priority
The priority CHECK rejects the urgent value
The work and home tags are created
A task-tag relationship cannot appear twice
Deleting a task deletes the related task_tags records
